extracted.intended_audience: public relations educators, writing researchers, and practitioners who pretest or craft PR messages
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for composing and pretesting public relations messages using cognitive-language principles (parsimony, redundancy, singularity, etc.) and the signaled stopping technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parsimony Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The fewer symbols used to communicate ideas or cognitive structures of the same complexity, the more efficiently the recipient can reconstruct the concept or cognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid wordiness: overuse of passive voice, complex and run-on sentences, and stacked modifiers violate parsimony. Note: a message can be parsimonious yet still unclear; parsimony must be balanced with clarity and redundancy where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redundancy Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of different symbols within the same symbol system or different symbol systems to communicate an idea increases accuracy and understanding, especially for complex messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce redundancy via definitions, analogies, metaphors, examples, parables, graphs, illustrations, formulas, or descriptive statistics to map new information onto familiar schemata. Excessive redundancy beyond the complexity of the message violates parsimony and can cause disinterest and reduced understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singularity Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: People find it easier to construct or reconstruct one cognitive structure at a time than two or more simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize writing with a unifying pattern (topic sentence followed by development and transitions). When multiple cognitions are necessary, separate them and link with clear transitional devices. Contrasting two cognitive structures at once often violates singularity and can cause confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complexity Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The greater the complexity of a cognitive structure or the schema to which it connects, the harder it is to communicate that cognition to someone without an appropriate schema.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know your audience’s cognitive complexities; choose symbol systems appropriate to readers. For complex ideas, map them into symbol systems or schemata familiar to the audience and consider additional redundancy or sequencing to aid reconstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low Involvement Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The lower a person's level of involvement in an issue, the stronger the effects of singularity, parsimony, clarity, redundancy, and complexity in achieving accuracy and understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For low-involvement audiences, simplify messages (singularity, parsimony, clarity) and add appropriate redundancy to increase understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstruction Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: When communication is relied upon to help construct cognitions, messages often must be rewritten or reconceptualized to achieve accuracy and understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iteratively revise messages based on how well recipients can reconstruct intended cognitive structures; reconstruction often requires applying parsimony, redundancy, and clarity principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedback Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Messages produced after receiving feedback from previous communicative efforts will result in greater accuracy and understanding than the first message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pretest and collect feedback (e.g., via signaled stopping) and incorporate it into message revisions. Feedback-based messaging is empirically superior to untested first drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitude Frame Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-situational attitudes or referent criteria provide frames for thought that can make it difficult to achieve accuracy and understanding for cognitions whose behavioral implications fall outside the attitude frame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect counterarguing when new information conflicts with existing attitude frames; consider framing strategies or additional redundancy to bridge attitude gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasion Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who holds a preponderance of favorable OR unfavorable cognitions (wedges) is likely to form an attitude and engage in behavior; a person with roughly equal favorable and unfavorable cognitions (hedges) is less likely to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increase the number of cognitive structures favoring the communicator's position to raise likelihood of attitude formation and behavior change; map persuasive elements onto schemata to create wedges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synecdochic Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols that suggest a familiar schema to the recipient evoke complex meaning that may not be apparent from the phrase alone to someone without a similar schema.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious using synecdochic phrases (e.g., using 'girls' to mean 'women') because they can decrease accuracy and understanding among recipients who lack the referenced schema.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication will achieve accuracy and understanding more often when recipients receive symbols that correspond to each element of a cognitive structure and when the organizational pattern of the message follows a rule apparent to the recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure symbols map clearly to intended cognitive elements and that organization (sequencing, topic sentences, transitions) is transparent to readers. Poor transitions or opaque organization reduce clarity and increase confusion stops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signaled Stopping Technique (SST) — method overview
rubrics_metrics.description: Carter's signaled stopping technique: experimental subjects read a message and place a slash mark where they stop reading for any reason; stops are then coded to infer cognitive processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SST to pretest messages and observe points that provoke confusion, rereading, insight, etc. The technique requires clear instructions, coding scheme, and careful experimental design; authors note SST is useful but may require refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signaled Stopping Coding Categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard coded reasons for stopping used in these studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C = Because of confusion (lost idea); R = To reread (go back to clarify or rehearse); Q = To ask a question (reader forms a question for the writer); T = To think (reflect/rehearse over what has been read); U = Because of sudden insight or understanding (registers main idea); Agree = reader agrees; D = To disagree. Studies sometimes allow writing in other reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pretesting / SST procedural best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural elements for running signaled stopping pretests with student subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Randomly assign materials (e.g., alternate copies), explain stopping categories with examples, provide an explanation sheet, assure voluntary participation and anonymity, state responses won't affect grades, and instruct subjects to ignore completion time differences. Note: better matching and tighter protocols recommended for stronger experimental control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing practices that violate parsimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific examples of writing choices that reduce parsimony and impede efficient reconstruction of cognitive structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overuse of passive voice, complex and run-on sentences, dependent clauses that disguise subject-object relations, and stacking modifiers which reduce redundancy and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical and explanatory devices that increase redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Devices that add redundancy and can increase accuracy and understanding when used appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include definitions, analogies, metaphors, examples, parables, graphs, illustrations, formulas, and descriptive statistics to map unfamiliar cognitions to familiar schemata; monitor for overuse which violates parsimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequencing and element placement guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequencing of story or message elements affects reader stopping patterns and understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange elements so outcomes follow causes (example: place absorption-rate info before stages of inebriation). Poor sequencing or abrupt contrasts can violate singularity and increase confusion; transitions can mitigate this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rereading as a comprehension strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Rereading stops often reflect constructive processes that aid conceptual abstraction and rehearsal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat purposeful rereading as generally positive for elaboration and long-term storage (understanding), but recognize that in cases where schemata do not match, rereading can lead to further confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: SST interpretation caution — role of examples/analogies
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings indicate stories with examples and analogies produced more stops (thinking, understanding) but few confusion stops; some contrasts in examples produced confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting SST results, consider interplay of parsimony and redundancy. Examples/analogies can increase understanding but certain contrasts (pro/con examples) may provoke confusion in some readers; refine materials and further test.
